title: Quiz: Individuals and Moving Range (I-MR) Charts

questions.text: Given x̄ = 100 ms and MR̄ = 10 ms, what is the UCL for the I-Chart?
questions.explanation: The I-Chart UCL = x̄ + E₂ × MR̄ = 100 + 2.66 × 10 = 126.6 ms. The constant E₂ = 2.66 is derived from d₂ = 1.128 for n=1.

questions.text: What does the Moving Range in an I-MR chart measure?
options: The absolute difference between consecutive individual observations
The standard deviation within a subgroup
The range within a subgroup of 5 measurements
questions.explanation: MRᵢ = |xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁|. It captures the short-term, point-to-point variability when subgroups of size n=1 are used.

questions.text: The I-MR chart is the best choice when manufacturing one batch per day and only one quality measurement is available per batch.
questions.explanation: When it is impossible or impractical to form subgroups (e.g., one batch per day), the I-MR chart is the correct choice — it handles individual observations.

questions.text: Why is the I-MR chart particularly valuable in Big Data streaming environments?
options: It handles very large subgroup sizes efficiently
It can process one observation at a time, making real-time monitoring possible
It requires no control chart constants
It is immune to outliers in the data
questions.explanation: In streaming systems (Kafka, Spark Streaming), data arrives one point at a time. The I-MR chart evaluates each new observation immediately, enabling real-time out-of-control detection.

questions.text: The LCL for the MR-Chart is always set to zero, even if the formula gives a negative number.
questions.explanation: Negative moving ranges are impossible (it is an absolute difference), so the MR-Chart LCL is always 0. D₃ = 0 for n=1, reflecting this.
